[high] Quoted by Asaṅga (4th-5th c.) and first translated into Chinese by Bodhiruci between 508 and 537 CE. (Potter 2003, Encyclopedia of Indian Philosophies, Vol. IX; Willis; Vinītā 2010, A unique collection of twenty Sūtras in a Sanskrit manuscript from the Potala)

[high] The earliest extant translation into Chinese (by Zhi Qian) provides a secure terminus ante quem of 223–228 CE. (Jonathan A. Silk et al. (eds.) 2015, Brill's Encyclopedia of Buddhism Vol I; Paul Williams (ed.) 2005, Buddhism - Critical Concepts in Religious Studies; Vol III)

[high] The work rTen 'brel bstod pa legs bshad snying po was composed during the lifetime of Tsongkhapa (1357–1419). (John Powers 1991, The Concept of the Ultimate (paramārtha) in the Samdhinirmocana-sūtra; Georges Dreyfus 2003, The Svātantrika-Prāsaṅgika Distinction)

[medium] Kikuya dates Buddhaśrījñāna (Jñānapāda) to ca. 750–800 CE, providing the floruit of the author and the composition window of his basic utpattikrama sādhana. (Kikuya 2012, Reconstruction of Jñānapāda's Caturaṅgasādhana-Samantabhadrī)

[high] The work was composed and translated into Tibetan by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna (active c. 982–1054 CE) in collaboration with Śākya blo gros. (Izumi Miyazaki (2007), 'Atiśa (Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna)—His Philosophy, Practice and its Sources')

[high] Atiśa arrived in Western Tibet in 1042 CE, where he composed the text at the request of Byaṅ chub 'od before passing away in Central Tibet in 1054 CE. (Seyfort Ruegg 2003, Problems in the Transmission of Vajrayāna; Brill's Encyclopedia of Buddhism Vol I, 2015)

[medium] Scholarship places Nāgārjuna between the last quarter of the 1st century and the 2nd century CE based on his synchronism with King Gautamīputra Śātakarṇi (r. c. 106+ CE). A firm terminus ante quem is  (Encyclopaedia of Buddhism, Vol. VIII (Weeraratne ed. 2007); Brill's Encyclopedia of Buddhism, Vol. I (Silk ed. 2015))

[high] Dated based on the lifetime of the author, Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna (982–1054 CE). (Miyazaki 2007, Atiśa (Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna)—His Philosophy, Practice and its Sources; Mochizuki, Der Bodhicitta-Abschnitt in Atiśas Ratnakaraṇḍodghāṭa)
[medium] Based on the biographical dates given in the secondary literature for Dīpaṃkara (Atiśa) of 980–1053 CE. (India’s Contribution to World Thought and Culture (1970))
[medium] Dated within the lifespan of Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna (982–1054), identified as the author. (Miyazaki 2007, Atiśa (Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna)—His Philosophy, Practice and its Sources)
[high] Dated directly based on the author Atiśa's lifespan (982–1054) as cited by Miyazaki. (Miyazaki 2007, Atiśa (Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna)—His Philosophy, Practice and its Sources)

[medium] Derived from the conventional lifespan assigned to the author Kamalaśīla (c. 740–795 CE) in secondary bibliography. (Napper 1985, Dependent-Arising and Emptiness; Lopez 1987, A Study of Svatantrika)

[medium] Traditionally attributed to the 6th-century Bhāviveka (ca. 490–570), but modern critical scholarship (Ejima, Seyfort Ruegg, Silk) generally considers it the work of a later 'pseudo-Bhāviveka' belongin (Iida 1980, Reason and Emptiness; Seyfort Ruegg 1982/1990, Towards a Chronology of the Madhyamaka School)

[high] The root work must predate its commentary by Candrakīrti (placed in the latter half of the 7th century) and its earliest Tibetan cataloguing (lHan-dkar catalogue, 824 CE). (Loizzo 2001; Loizzo 2007)

[medium] Attributed to Vasubandhu (Old Vasubandhu, c. 320–380 CE according to Frauwallner/Péri) and translated into Chinese by Kumārajīva (in China 401–413 CE). (Lee 2001, A Study of Vasubandhu -With special reference to the Vyākhyāyukti-)

[medium] Commentator Sthiramati flourished in the 6th century, placing the composition of the Pañcaskandhaka no later than the 6th century. (Jowita Kramer (2013), Sthiramati's Pañcaskandhakavibhāṣā, Part 1: Critical edition)

[high] Śubhagupta flourished between the mid-7th and late 8th century (ca. 650–750 according to Hattori, or 720–780 according to Frauwallner), active after Dharmakīrti and cited by Śāntarakṣita and Kamalaśīl (Hattori 1960, Bāhyārthasiddhikārikā of Śubhagupta; Steinkellner and Much 1995, Texte der erkenntnistheoretischen Schule des Buddhismus; Mikogami 1986, シュバグプタの Bāhyārthasiddhikārikā)

[medium] The passages state that the work depends on 2nd-3rd century sūtras and was commented upon by Vasubandhu (placed c. 320-400 or fl. 360). (Dan Cozort, dissert. 1989; Jeffrey Hopkins 1999, Emptiness in the Mind-Only School of Buddhism)

[medium] Potter lists the work around 253 CE; Harivarman was a pupil of Kumāralāta (mid-3rd century CE); and the work was translated into Chinese by Kumārajīva at the beginning of the 5th century CE. (Potter 1999, Encyclopedia of Indian Philosophies, Vol. VIII; Kajiyama 1978-84)

[medium] Scholars suggest either the 2nd century (if composed by the Ghoṣaka of the Mahāvibhāṣā) or the 3rd century prior to its Chinese translation, dated to the Wei/Wu period (ca. 220–280 CE). (Willemen, Dessein & Cox (1998), Sarvāstivāda Buddhist Scholasticism; La Vallée Poussin (1923), L'Abhidharmakośa de Vasubandhu)

[medium] The Sanskrit text is attributed to Nāgārjuna, but the only hard terminus ante quem provided in the text is the Tibetan translation executed by Dpal brtsegs and Ye shes snying po (Jñānagarbha) around c (Harrison and Schopen ed. 1998, Sūryacandrāya)

[high] Attributed to Dignāga (fl. late 5th century / c. 400–550 CE; Potter places the work c. 510 CE). A firm terminus ante quem is provided by Paramārtha's Chinese translation executed between 557 and 569 C (Banerjee 1980, Bulletin of Tibetology 16 (1–3); Potter 2003, Encyclopedia of Indian Philosophies, Vol. IX; Steinkellner and Much 1995, Texte der erkenntnistheoretischen Schule des Buddhismus)

[high] Dignāga is dated to c. 400–550 CE (or late 5th century CE), and the text was translated into Chinese by Paramārtha between 557 and 569 CE, which provides a strict terminus ante quem. (Banerjee 1980, Bulletin of Tibetology Nos. 1-3; Potter 2003, Encyclopedia of Indian Philosophies, Vol. IX; Steinkellner & Much 1995, Texte der erkenntnistheoretischen Schule des Buddhismus)

[high] Covers the range of scholarly dating for the author Dharmakīrti (ca. 600–660 per Frauwallner, with alternate estimates from ca. 530–600 and 550–620 cited in Steinkellner & Much). (Steinkellner and Much 1995, Texte der erkenntnistheoretischen Schule des Buddhismus)

[high] The terminus ante quem is established by the Chinese translation by Paramārtha (dated 549, 550, or 552–557 CE). The text is widely recognized as a pre-Dignāga work not much older than Vasubandhu. (Uwe Frankenhauser 1996, Die Einführung der buddhistischen Logik in China; E. Steinkellner und M. T. Much 1995, Texte der erkenntnistheoretischen Schule des Buddhismus; Giuseppe Tucci 1929, Pre-Diṅnāga)

[high] The terminus ante quem is established by the Chinese translation dated to the fourth quarter of the 5th century. (Steinkellner and Much 1995, Texte der erkenntnistheoretischen Schule des Buddhismus; Franco 2004, Xuanzang's proof of idealism)

[high] Based on the established lifespan of the author Jitāri (ca. 940–1000 CE; or ca. 940–980 CE per Vidyabhusan), combined with the mid-11th century terminus ante quem provided by the Tibetan translation. (Steinkellner and Much 1995, Texte der erkenntnistheoretischen Schule des Buddhismus; Rangaswami Iyengar 1952, Tarkabhāṣa and Vādasthāna of Mokṣākaragupta and Jitāripāda)

[high] Based on scholarly estimates for the author Dharmakīrti's lifetime spanning ca. 530-600 (Lindtner), ca. 550-620 (Kimura), to ca. 600-660 (Frauwallner). (Steinkellner and Much 1995, Texte der erkenntnistheoretischen Schule des Buddhismus)
